/*
 * PROGRAM:     memfd Anonymous Shared-Memory Demo (parent + child)
 * MECHANISM:   Linux memfd_create() + mmap(MAP_SHARED) + anonymous pipe for
 *              parent↔child synchronization
 * DESCRIPTION: Demonstrates parent→child one-way communication via an
 *              anonymous, RAM-backed shared memory region created with the
 *              Linux-specific memfd_create() syscall.  Unlike shm_open() or
 *              a regular file, a memfd object has NO name in the filesystem
 *              or the POSIX SHM namespace — it is only reachable via its
 *              file descriptor, which the child inherits across fork().
 *              Because shared-memory writes are not inherently ordered with
 *              respect to another process' reads, the program also creates
 *              an ordinary anonymous pipe and uses it as a synchronization
 *              primitive: the parent writes a single byte AFTER it has
 *              finished writing the shared region, and the child blocks in
 *              read() on the pipe until that byte arrives — guaranteeing
 *              the child only inspects the mapping after parent writes are
 *              fully visible.  The parent then waitpid()s for the child.
 * USAGE:       Compile:  make memfd_demo   (or `gcc -o memfd_demo memfd_demo.c`)
 *              Run:      ./memfd_demo [optional_message]
 *              No partner program is needed — both sides are fork() children
 *              of this single executable.  Requires Linux ≥ 3.17 for
 *              memfd_create().
 * STEPS:       ① Ignore SIGPIPE for the sync pipe's EPIPE-safe writes
 *              ② memfd_create() an anonymous file, ftruncate to MAP_SIZE
 *              ③ mmap(MAP_SHARED) the memfd into BOTH parent+child address space
 *              ④ pipe() for synchronization, then fork()
 *              ⑤ CHILD:  close pipe write-end, read sync byte, scan mapping
 *                         for NUL, print string, _exit(status)
 *              ⑥ PARENT: close pipe read-end, fill mapping with message,
 *                         write sync byte, close write-end, waitpid(child)
 *              ⑦ Both sides munmap() the region and close the memfd
 */

#define MAP_SIZE 4096U                    /* size of the shared memfd region */

/*
 * child_process — code exclusively executed by the forked child.
 *
 * The child's job is:
 *   1. Close the pipe write-end immediately (we inherited both ends).
 *   2. Block in read() on the pipe read-end until the parent sends the
 *      "I'm done writing shared memory" synchronization byte.
 *   3. Only then scan the shared mapping for a NUL terminator and print
 *      the bounded string to stdout.
 *   4. Clean up ALL resources the child inherited and terminate with
 *      _exit() — NOT exit() — to avoid flushing parent stdio buffers twice
 *      (an unflushed parent buffer is copied into the child at fork()).
 *
 * Parameters:
 *   memfd   — inherited file descriptor referring to the memfd object.
 *   mapping — inherited virtual-address mapping of that memfd object.
 *   pipefd  — inherited two-int array for the sync pipe;
 *             pipefd[0] = read end, pipefd[1] = write end.
 *
 * Does NOT return; terminates the child process via _exit(status).
 */
static void child_process(int memfd, const char *mapping, int pipefd[2])
{
    char signal_byte;
    ssize_t received;
    const char *terminator;
    int status = EXIT_FAILURE;

    if (close(pipefd[1]) == -1) {
        perror("child close pipe write end");
        goto cleanup;
    }
    pipefd[1] = -1;

    /*
     * Block waiting for the parent's synchronization signal.
     *
     * Without this read() the child could start scanning the mapping
     * before the parent has finished writing into it — a classic
     * read-before-write data race.  Because the sync pipe's read()
     * returns only AFTER the parent has called write() on the other
     * end, and pipe write↔read is ordered by the kernel with all
     * preceding user-space stores on the same CPU, this acts as a
     * portable acquire barrier.
     */
    do {
        received = read(pipefd[0], &signal_byte, 1);
    } while (received == -1 && errno == EINTR);
    if (received == -1) {
        perror("child read synchronization pipe");
        goto cleanup;
    }
    if (received != 1) {
        fprintf(stderr, "child: 父进程未发送写入完成信号\n");
        goto cleanup;
    }

    /*
     * At this point we are guaranteed the parent has finished writing
     * the mapping.  Scan for a NUL terminator strictly within MAP_SIZE
     * bytes; memchr() protects us from overrunning the page even if the
     * writer forgot to include a terminator.
     */
    terminator = memchr(mapping, '\0', MAP_SIZE);
    if (terminator == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "child: memfd 中没有合法的字符串终止符\n");
        goto cleanup;
    }
    if (printf("子进程读取 memfd：%.*s\n",
               (int)(terminator - mapping), mapping) < 0 ||
        fflush(stdout) == EOF) {
        perror("child output");
        goto cleanup;
    }
    status = EXIT_SUCCESS;

cleanup:
    if (munmap((void *)mapping, MAP_SIZE) == -1) {
        perror("child munmap");
        status = EXIT_FAILURE;
    }
    if (pipefd[0] != -1 && close(pipefd[0]) == -1) {
        perror("child close pipe read end");
        status = EXIT_FAILURE;
    }
    if (pipefd[1] != -1 && close(pipefd[1]) == -1) {
        perror("child close pipe write end");
        status = EXIT_FAILURE;
    }
    if (close(memfd) == -1) {
        perror("child close memfd");
        status = EXIT_FAILURE;
    }
    _exit(status);
}

int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
    const char *message = argc > 1 ? argv[1] : "父进程通过 memfd 写入的消息";
    size_t message_len = strlen(message);
    int memfd = -1;
    char *mapping = MAP_FAILED;
    int pipefd[2] = {-1, -1};            /* sync pipe: [0]=read, [1]=write */
    pid_t child = -1;
    pid_t waited;
    int child_status = 0;
    int status = EXIT_FAILURE;
    char signal_byte = 'R';              /* arbitrary value; any byte works */
    ssize_t sent;
    struct sigaction action;

    if (message_len >= MAP_SIZE) {
        fprintf(stderr, "消息过长，最多允许 %u 字节（需保留结尾空字符）\n",
                MAP_SIZE - 1U);
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    /*
     * ① Ignore SIGPIPE.
     *
     * If the child exits abnormally and closes its pipe read-end before we
     * write signal_byte, the kernel would normally deliver SIGPIPE (default
     * action = kill process).  Ignoring SIGPIPE converts that event into an
     * EPIPE return from write(), which our cleanup path handles gracefully
     * and reports to the user.
     */
    memset(&action, 0, sizeof(action));
    action.sa_handler = SIG_IGN;
    if (sigemptyset(&action.sa_mask) == -1 ||
        sigaction(SIGPIPE, &action, NULL) == -1) {
        perror("sigaction SIGPIPE");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    /*
     * ② memfd_create() — Linux-specific anonymous file.
     *
     * memfd_create() returns a file descriptor that refers to a newly
     * created, zero-length, RAM-backed (tmpfs) anonymous file.  The name
     * string is only used for /proc/<pid>/fd/ debugging display and has
     * no semantic meaning.  MFD_CLOEXEC marks the fd so it won't leak
     * across exec(), but it will still be inherited across fork() —
     * that's exactly how the child receives the shared region in this
     * demo.  We then ftruncate() to MAP_SIZE bytes just like any other
     * mmap-able fd.
     */
    memfd = memfd_create("ipc_memfd_demo", MFD_CLOEXEC);
    if (memfd == -1) {
        perror("memfd_create");
        goto cleanup;
    }
    if (ftruncate(memfd, (off_t)MAP_SIZE) == -1) {
        perror("ftruncate");
        goto cleanup;
    }

    /*
     * ③ Map the memfd MAP_SHARED, then create the sync pipe, then fork().
     *
     * Order matters: both mmap() and pipe() must succeed BEFORE fork()
     * because the child inherits their results.  MAP_SHARED is essential
     * for the child to observe parent writes; MAP_PRIVATE would cause
     * copy-on-write duplication with no IPC visibility.
     */
    mapping = mmap(NULL, MAP_SIZE, PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE,
                   MAP_SHARED, memfd, 0);
    if (mapping == MAP_FAILED) {
        perror("mmap");
        goto cleanup;
    }
    if (pipe(pipefd) == -1) {
        perror("pipe");
        goto cleanup;
    }

    child = fork();
    if (child == -1) {
        perror("fork");
        goto cleanup;
    }
    if (child == 0) {
        /* Child branch: never returns. */
        child_process(memfd, mapping, pipefd);
    }

    /* ------------------------------ PARENT ------------------------------ */

    /* Parent will only WRITE the sync pipe; close inherited read-end now. */
    if (close(pipefd[0]) == -1) {
        perror("parent close pipe read end");
        pipefd[0] = -1;
        goto wait_for_child;
    }
    pipefd[0] = -1;

    /*
     * ④ Parent populates the shared region.
     *
     * memset first zeroes the full page (NUL-fill = empty default string),
     * then memcpy copies the message bytes AND its trailing NUL terminator
     * into offset 0.  After these stores complete we write signal_byte
     * into the pipe; when the child's read() returns, the child is
     * guaranteed to observe all prior stores into the mapping.
     */
    memset(mapping, 0, MAP_SIZE);
    memcpy(mapping, message, message_len + 1U);

    do {
        sent = write(pipefd[1], &signal_byte, 1);
    } while (sent == -1 && errno == EINTR);
    if (sent == -1) {
        perror("parent write synchronization pipe");
        goto wait_for_child;
    }
    if (sent != 1) {
        fprintf(stderr, "parent: 同步信号未完整写入\n");
        goto wait_for_child;
    }

    /* Closing the pipe write-end also signals EOF to the child's reader. */
    if (close(pipefd[1]) == -1) {
        perror("parent close pipe write end");
        pipefd[1] = -1;
        goto wait_for_child;
    }
    pipefd[1] = -1;

wait_for_child:
    /* Ensure both pipe ends are really closed before we wait. */
    if (pipefd[1] != -1) {
        if (close(pipefd[1]) == -1) {
            perror("parent close pipe write end");
        }
        pipefd[1] = -1;
    }

    /*
     * ⑤ waitpid() for the child to finish.
     *
     * Retry on EINTR (signal handlers installed elsewhere could fire).
     * We consider the overall demo successful only if the child exited
     * normally with EXIT_SUCCESS.
     */
    do {
        waited = waitpid(child, &child_status, 0);
    } while (waited == -1 && errno == EINTR);
    if (waited == -1) {
        perror("waitpid");
        goto cleanup;
    }
    if (!WIFEXITED(child_status) || WEXITSTATUS(child_status) != EXIT_SUCCESS) {
        fprintf(stderr, "子进程读取 memfd 失败\n");
        goto cleanup;
    }

    printf("父进程已写入并等待子进程读取完成\n");
    status = EXIT_SUCCESS;

cleanup:
    if (pipefd[0] != -1 && close(pipefd[0]) == -1) {
        perror("close pipe read end");
        status = EXIT_FAILURE;
    }
    if (pipefd[1] != -1 && close(pipefd[1]) == -1) {
        perror("close pipe write end");
        status = EXIT_FAILURE;
    }
    if (mapping != MAP_FAILED && munmap(mapping, MAP_SIZE) == -1) {
        perror("munmap");
        status = EXIT_FAILURE;
    }
    if (memfd != -1 && close(memfd) == -1) {
        perror("close memfd");
        status = EXIT_FAILURE;
    }
    /*
     * Closing the last fd that refers to a memfd object automatically
     * releases the underlying RAM pages — no separate shm_unlink() or
     * filesystem removal step is needed.  This is one of memfd's nicest
     * properties vs. POSIX SHM / SYSV SHM / regular-file mmap.
     */
    return status;
}

/*
 * PROGRAM:     System V Shared Memory Reader (shmget + shmat)
 * MECHANISM:   System V (SYSV / AT&T) shared memory segment
 *              (ftok → shmget → shmctl IPC_STAT → shmat → read → shmdt → IPC_RMID)
 * DESCRIPTION: The READER / CONSUMER half of a System V shared-memory demo.
 *              Re-derives the same SYSV IPC key used by the writer via
 *              ftok("/tmp/ipc_sysv_shm_demo.key", 'S'), opens the segment
 *              the writer created with shmget(), verifies its size via
 *              shmctl(IPC_STAT), attaches read-only with shmat(SHM_RDONLY),
 *              scans for a NUL terminator within the SHM_SIZE region, and
 *              prints the bounded string.  As the lifecycle owner it then
 *              removes the segment with shmctl(IPC_RMID) and unlinks the
 *              anchor key file so the next demo run begins from a clean
 *              state.
 * USAGE:       1. Run the writer first (creates key file and segment):
 *                  ./sysv_shm_writer [optional_message]
 *              2. Immediately afterward, run THIS reader:
 *                  ./sysv_shm_reader
 * STEPS:       ① prepare_key_file() → open/validate the ftok anchor
 *              ② ftok() → same key_t the writer used
 *              ③ shmget() existing segment, shmctl(IPC_STAT) verify size
 *              ④ shmat(SHM_RDONLY) → memchr(NUL) → bounded printf
 *              ⑤ shmdt, shmctl(IPC_RMID) the segment, unlink the key file
 */

#define KEY_FILE   "/tmp/ipc_sysv_shm_demo.key"  /* ftok() anchor file path */
#define PROJECT_ID 'S'                           /* matches writer proj_id */
#define SHM_SIZE   4096U                         /* segment size expected   */

/*
 * prepare_key_file — create/validate ftok() anchor; see sysv_shm_writer.c.
 */
static int prepare_key_file(void)
{
    int fd = open(KEY_FILE, O_CREAT | O_RDWR | O_CLOEXEC | O_NOFOLLOW, 0600);
    struct stat file_info;

    if (fd == -1) {
        return -1;
    }
    if (fstat(fd, &file_info) == -1) {
        int saved_errno = errno;
        (void)close(fd);
        errno = saved_errno;
        return -1;
    }
    if (!S_ISREG(file_info.st_mode) || file_info.st_uid != geteuid()) {
        (void)close(fd);
        errno = EPERM;
        return -1;
    }
    if (fchmod(fd, 0600) == -1) {
        int saved_errno = errno;
        (void)close(fd);
        errno = saved_errno;
        return -1;
    }
    if (close(fd) == -1) {
        return -1;
    }
    return 0;
}

int main(void)
{
    key_t key;
    int shmid = -1;
    struct shmid_ds segment_info;          /* output of shmctl(IPC_STAT)     */
    const char *mapping = (void *)-1;     /* shmat pointer; (void*)-1 = err  */
    const char *terminator;               /* NUL byte position inside mapping */
    int key_ready = 0;
    int segment_found = 0;
    int status = EXIT_FAILURE;

    /*
     * ① Prepare the ftok() anchor file.
     *
     * The reader must derive exactly the same key_t integer the writer
     * produced.  That requires the same KEY_FILE pathname and PROJECT_ID
     * byte, plus the KEY_FILE must still refer to the same inode as when
     * the writer ran.  prepare_key_file() hardens the anchor against
     * symlink attacks and wrong ownership before we rely on it.
     */
    if (prepare_key_file() == -1) {
        perror("prepare key file");
        goto cleanup;
    }
    key_ready = 1;

    key = ftok(KEY_FILE, PROJECT_ID);
    if (key == (key_t)-1) {
        perror("ftok");
        goto cleanup;
    }

    /*
     * ② Open the existing segment.
     *
     * With no IPC_CREAT flag, shmget() will fail with ENOENT if the
     * writer hasn't run yet (or its own segment has already been IPC_RMID
     * removed).  size=0 means "open the segment no matter what its actual
     * size is" — we validate the real size in the next step using
     * shmctl(IPC_STAT).  Mode 0600 is the owner read/write permission
     * mask the writer created the segment with.
     */
    shmid = shmget(key, 0, 0600);
    if (shmid == -1) {
        perror("shmget");
        goto cleanup;
    }
    segment_found = 1;

    /*
     * ③ Confirm the segment is at least SHM_SIZE bytes long.
     *
     * Without this check, a malicious local program could create a
     * smaller SYSV SHM segment at the same key and trick us into
     * attaching it; we'd then read beyond shm_segsz and SIGSEGV when we
     * hit the end of the pages the kernel actually allocated.
     */
    if (shmctl(shmid, IPC_STAT, &segment_info) == -1) {
        perror("shmctl IPC_STAT");
        goto cleanup;
    }
    if (segment_info.shm_segsz < SHM_SIZE) {
        fprintf(stderr, "System V 共享内存段长度不足 %u 字节\n", SHM_SIZE);
        goto cleanup;
    }

    /*
     * ④ Attach read-only with SHM_RDONLY.
     *
     * SHM_RDONLY is the SysV analog of mmap(PROT_READ).  Even if the
     * segment's mode bits allow writing (they do: 0600 and we are the
     * owner), the reader side explicitly opts in to read-only so a stray
     * pointer write in the reader can't corrupt the shared data.
     */
    mapping = shmat(shmid, NULL, SHM_RDONLY);
    if (mapping == (void *)-1) {
        perror("shmat");
        goto cleanup;
    }

    /*
     * The System V shm* API does not store any user-defined length on a
     * per-message basis, so our demo protocol is simply "a NUL-terminated
     * C string stored at offset 0".  Bounded memchr() inside the segment
     * protects us from a writer that omitted the NUL or crashed mid
     * write.
     */
    terminator = memchr(mapping, '\0', SHM_SIZE);
    if (terminator == NULL) {
        fprintf(stderr, "共享内存中没有合法的字符串终止符\n");
        goto cleanup;
    }
    printf("读取到 System V 共享内存：%.*s\n",
           (int)(terminator - mapping), mapping);
    status = EXIT_SUCCESS;

cleanup:
    /* Detach even on error paths; avoid leaking attach references. */
    if (mapping != (void *)-1 && shmdt(mapping) == -1) {
        perror("shmdt");
        status = EXIT_FAILURE;
    }
    /*
     * ⑤ Remove the segment and the key file.
     *
     * As the consumer / lifecycle-owner the reader always removes the
     * segment, even if reading failed — a failed demo shouldn't leak a
     * kernel-persistent SYSV IPC object (SYSV objects survive until
     * explicit IPC_RMID or OS reboot).  EINVAL / EIDRM mean another
     * process already removed it between our shmget and now, so those
     * errnos are ignored.
     *
     * The key file is also unlinked; the writer will recreate it on the
     * next demo run.
     */
    if (segment_found && shmctl(shmid, IPC_RMID, NULL) == -1 &&
        errno != EINVAL && errno != EIDRM) {
        perror("shmctl IPC_RMID");
        status = EXIT_FAILURE;
    }
    if (key_ready && unlink(KEY_FILE) == -1 && errno != ENOENT) {
        perror("unlink key file");
        status = EXIT_FAILURE;
    }
    return status;
}

#define _POSIX_C_SOURCE 200809L

#include <errno.h>
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <sys/ipc.h>
#include <sys/shm.h>
#include <sys/stat.h>
#include <unistd.h>

/*
 * PROGRAM:     System V Shared Memory Writer (shmget + shmat)
 * MECHANISM:   System V (SYSV / AT&T) shared memory segment
 *              (ftok → shmget[IPC_CREAT|IPC_EXCL] → shmat → write → shmdt)
 * DESCRIPTION: The WRITER / CREATOR half of a System V shared-memory demo.
 *              System V IPC objects are identified by `key_t` integers
 *              produced by ftok() from a regular filesystem anchor file and
 *              a project-ID byte.  This program first creates/validates the
 *              anchor file at /tmp/ipc_sysv_shm_demo.key (ensures it is a
 *              regular file owned by us, mode 0600), derives a key via
 *              ftok(), then creates a new 4 KiB SYSV SHM segment with
 *              IPC_CREAT|IPC_EXCL (removing any stale segment left by a
 *              crashed prior run).  It attaches the segment, zero-fills it,
 *              copies in a NUL-terminated Chinese greeting, detaches, and
 *              leaves the segment present for sysv_shm_reader to consume.
 *              Optional command-line argument overrides the default message.
 * USAGE:       1. Run writer first (creates key file + SHM segment):
 *                  ./sysv_shm_writer [optional_message]
 *              2. In another terminal, run the reader:
 *                  ./sysv_shm_reader
 *              Reader removes both the SYSV segment and the key file.
 * STEPS:       ① Validate message length
 *              ② prepare_key_file(): create or reuse anchor file + harden it
 *              ③ ftok() → integer key
 *              ④ shmget(IPC_CREAT|IPC_EXCL); clear any stale segment on EEXIST
 *              ⑤ shmat() → memset(0) → memcpy(msg + NUL) → shmdt()
 *              ⑥ On failure only: shmctl(IPC_RMID) + unlink key file
 */

#define KEY_FILE   "/tmp/ipc_sysv_shm_demo.key"  /* ftok() anchor file path */
#define PROJECT_ID 'S'                           /* 8-bit project ID for ftok */
#define SHM_SIZE   4096U                         /* one page, demo capacity */

/*
 * prepare_key_file — create/validate the filesystem anchor for ftok().
 *
 * ftok() computes a key_t from (st_dev, st_ino, low-8-bits-of-project_id).
 * If a bad actor replaced KEY_FILE with a symlink or a file owned by another
 * uid, we would derive the same key as some unrelated IPC object and risk
 * either permission denials OR writing into a stranger's shared memory.  We
 * therefore:
 *   • open with O_CREAT | O_EXCL | O_CLOEXEC | O_NOFOLLOW if possible, else
 *     fall back to O_RDONLY when the file already exists (EEXIST).
 *   • fstat() to confirm it's a regular file (S_ISREG) owned by our euid.
 *   • fchmod() to 0600 so no other user can read/write the anchor.
 *   • close the fd when done.
 *
 * Parameters:
 *   created — output flag; set to 1 if we actually created a new file,
 *             0 if we reused an existing one.  Caller uses this flag during
 *             cleanup so only freshly-created files are removed on error.
 *
 * Return: 0 on success, -1 on any failure (errno preserved; caller uses
 *         perror() with a suitable prefix).
 */
static int prepare_key_file(void)
{
    int fd = open(KEY_FILE, O_CREAT | O_RDWR | O_CLOEXEC | O_NOFOLLOW, 0600);
    struct stat file_info;

    if (fd == -1) {
        return -1;
    }
    if (fstat(fd, &file_info) == -1) {
        int saved_errno = errno;
        (void)close(fd);
        errno = saved_errno;
        return -1;
    }
    if (!S_ISREG(file_info.st_mode) || file_info.st_uid != geteuid()) {
        /* Either not a regular file, or another user owns it → unsafe. */
        (void)close(fd);
        errno = EPERM;
        return -1;
    }
    if (fchmod(fd, 0600) == -1) {
        int saved_errno = errno;
        (void)close(fd);
        errno = saved_errno;
        return -1;
    }
    if (close(fd) == -1) {
        return -1;
    }
    return 0;
}

int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
    const char *message = argc > 1 ? argv[1] : "来自 System V 共享内存 writer 的消息";
    size_t message_len = strlen(message);
    key_t key;
    int shmid = -1;                       /* SYSV SHM segment identifier    */
    char *mapping = (void *)-1;           /* attach pointer (shmat returns -1 on error) */
    int segment_created = 0;              /* 1 after successful shmget(CREAT) */
    int key_ready = 0;                    /* 1 after prepare_key_file() OK   */
    int status = EXIT_FAILURE;            /* pessimistic default             */

    if (message_len >= SHM_SIZE) {
        fprintf(stderr, "消息过长，最多允许 %u 字节（需保留结尾空字符）\n",
                SHM_SIZE - 1U);
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    /*
     * ② Create/validate the ftok() anchor file.
     *
     * System V IPC cannot simply use a pathname (that's the POSIX SHM API).
     * Instead you convert a (pathname, proj_id) pair into a key_t integer
     * via ftok().  The anchor file MUST exist or ftok() fails with ENOENT.
     */
    if (prepare_key_file() == -1) {
        perror("prepare key file");
        goto cleanup;
    }
    key_ready = 1;

    /*
     * ③ Derive the SYSV IPC key from (KEY_FILE, PROJECT_ID).
     *
     * The same (pathname, proj_id) pair always yields the same key as long
     * as the pathname refers to the same inode — so both sides of the IPC
     * pair use identical KEY_FILE and PROJECT_ID defines.
     */
    key = ftok(KEY_FILE, PROJECT_ID);
    if (key == (key_t)-1) {
        perror("ftok");
        goto cleanup;
    }

    /*
     * ④ Create the shared memory segment exclusively.
     *
     * shmget(key, size, flags) either creates a new segment or looks up an
     * existing one based on IPC_CREAT / IPC_EXCL in `flags`.  With
     * IPC_CREAT|IPC_EXCL we demand a fresh segment; EEXIST means a prior
     * crashed run of this demo left a segment behind, so we locate it with
     * a plain shmget(key, 0, perms), destroy it with shmctl(IPC_RMID), and
     * retry the creation path so the reader is guaranteed to see the
     * correct freshly-written content rather than stale bytes.
     */
    shmid = shmget(key, SHM_SIZE, IPC_CREAT | IPC_EXCL | 0600);
    if (shmid == -1 && errno == EEXIST) {
        int stale_id = shmget(key, 0, 0600);
        if (stale_id == -1) {
            perror("shmget stale segment");
            goto cleanup;
        }
        if (shmctl(stale_id, IPC_RMID, NULL) == -1) {
            perror("shmctl IPC_RMID stale segment");
            goto cleanup;
        }
        shmid = shmget(key, SHM_SIZE, IPC_CREAT | IPC_EXCL | 0600);
    }
    if (shmid == -1) {
        perror("shmget");
        goto cleanup;
    }
    segment_created = 1;

    /*
     * ⑤ Attach the segment to our address space.
     *
     * shmat(shmid, NULL, 0) with NULL address lets the kernel pick a free
     * virtual address (the portable choice).  A zero `shmflg` grants both
     * read and write access (since the segment was created with mode 0600
     * and we are the owner).
     *
     * Note: shmat() returns (void *)-1 on error, NOT NULL — that's why we
     * initialized `mapping` to (void *)-1 instead of MAP_FAILED (which is
     * the mmap() convention).
     */
    mapping = shmat(shmid, NULL, 0);
    if (mapping == (void *)-1) {
        perror("shmat");
        goto cleanup;
    }

    memset(mapping, 0, SHM_SIZE);
    memcpy(mapping, message, message_len + 1U);
    printf("已写入 System V 共享内存：%s\n", message);
    status = EXIT_SUCCESS;

cleanup:
    /* Detach on any path; the segment itself persists in the kernel. */
    if (mapping != (void *)-1 && shmdt(mapping) == -1) {
        perror("shmdt");
        status = EXIT_FAILURE;
    }
    /*
     * ⑥ Only destroy resources on the FAILURE path.
     *
     * On SUCCESS the segment and key file are left intact for the reader
     * to consume.  On failure we clean up exactly the resources that
     * *this* invocation created — segment_created/key_ready flags track
     * that so we don't accidentally blow away files/segments created by
     * another cooperating process.
     */
    if (status != EXIT_SUCCESS && segment_created &&
        shmctl(shmid, IPC_RMID, NULL) == -1 &&
        errno != EINVAL && errno != EIDRM) {
        perror("shmctl IPC_RMID cleanup");
    }
    if (status != EXIT_SUCCESS && key_ready &&
        unlink(KEY_FILE) == -1 && errno != ENOENT) {
        perror("unlink key file cleanup");
    }
    return status;
}

#define _POSIX_C_SOURCE 200809L

#include <errno.h>
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <mqueue.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <sys/stat.h>

/*
 * PROGRAM:     POSIX Message Queue Receiver (mq_open / mq_receive / mq_unlink)
 * MECHANISM:   POSIX message queue (mqd_t) — priority-ordered, message-boundary
 *              preserving IPC created by the sender program above.
 * DESCRIPTION: The RECEIVER / CLEANER-UPPER half of the POSIX MQ demo.
 *              Opens the queue "/ipc_posix_mq_demo" read-only (O_RDONLY +
 *              blocking mode) and blocks in mq_receive() until the sender
 *              enqueues a message.  mq_receive() returns the number of bytes
 *              in the single discrete message that was dequeued, and writes
 *              the message's priority into the unsigned int output pointer
 *              (the 4th argument).  Because POSIX MQs are priority queues,
 *              if multiple messages with different priorities were queued we
 *              receive the numerically HIGHEST priority one first.  After
 *              printing the message and its priority the program closes the
 *              descriptor and calls mq_unlink() to remove the queue name
 *              from the kernel's MQ namespace so the next sender will create
 *              a fresh queue.  Link with -lrt on glibc systems.
 * USAGE:       1. ./posix_mq_sender [message]   in terminal A (creates queue)
 *              2. ./posix_mq_receiver           in terminal B (consumes + unlinks)
 *              Running the receiver first is valid: it simply blocks in
 *              mq_receive() with O_RDONLY until a writer calls mq_send().
 * STEPS:       ① mq_open(QUEUE_NAME, O_RDONLY) — no O_CREAT, reuse sender's queue
 *              ② mq_getattr() to confirm mq_msgsize matches our receive buffer
 *              ③ blocking mq_receive() loop (retry EINTR), capture length + priority
 *              ④ print length-prefixed bytes as a string, priority label to stdout
 *              ⑤ mq_close() descriptor + mq_unlink(QUEUE_NAME) to tear down name
 */

#define QUEUE_NAME    "/ipc_posix_mq_demo"   /* must match sender's name       */
#define MESSAGE_SIZE  256                    /* must match sender's mq_msgsize */

int main(void)
{
    char buffer[MESSAGE_SIZE + 1];           /* +1 for demo-only NUL appending */
    unsigned int priority = 0;
    ssize_t bytes_received = -1;
    int status = EXIT_FAILURE;

    /*
     * ① Open the existing queue read-only / blocking.
     *
     * We intentionally do NOT pass O_CREAT: if the queue doesn't exist
     * yet (receiver started before sender) mq_open fails with ENOENT —
     * the user should launch the sender first.  On glibc POSIX MQs have
     * NO special "both ends must be present" open-blocking semantics
     * like a FIFO, so a reader on an empty queue just blocks inside
     * mq_receive() later, NOT here.
     */
    mqd_t queue = mq_open(QUEUE_NAME, O_RDONLY);
    if (queue == (mqd_t)-1) {
        perror("mq_open");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    /*
     * ② Sanity-check attributes so our buffer isn't too small.
     *
     * POSIX requires mq_receive(msg_len) >= queue's mq_msgsize, otherwise
     * the call fails with EMSGSIZE and the message stays in the queue.
     * Doing this check first produces a friendlier diagnostic.
     */
    struct mq_attr attr;
    if (mq_getattr(queue, &attr) == -1) {
        perror("mq_getattr");
        goto cleanup_close;
    }
    if (attr.mq_msgsize > MESSAGE_SIZE) {
        fprintf(stderr, "发送端消息队列大小 (%ld) 超过接收缓冲区 (%d)\n",
                (long)attr.mq_msgsize, MESSAGE_SIZE);
        goto cleanup_close;
    }

    /*
     * ③ Block in mq_receive() until one message arrives.
     *
     * mq_receive() semantics (key difference from stream sockets):
     *   • RETURNS EXACTLY ONE message per call (no partial reads).
     *   • If multiple messages are queued, they are dequeued in order of
     *     DESCENDING priority, and within the same priority in FIFO order.
     *   • On success the return value is the length of that single message,
     *     the bytes land in buffer[0..n-1], and the 4th arg receives the
     *     priority the original sender passed to mq_send().
     *   • For EINTR we loop again as always.
     */
    for (;;) {
        bytes_received = mq_receive(queue, buffer, MESSAGE_SIZE, &priority);
        if (bytes_received >= 0)
            break;
        if (errno == EINTR)
            continue;
        perror("mq_receive");
        goto cleanup_close;
    }

    /*
     * mq_receive does NOT NUL-terminate the buffer (it stores exactly the
     * bytes the sender sent, nothing more).  In our demo the sending side
     * sends raw string bytes with no implicit terminator, so we append
     * our own '\0' bounded by MESSAGE_SIZE only for printf("%s") safety.
     */
    buffer[bytes_received] = '\0';
    printf("收到（优先级 %u，%zd 字节）：%s\n",
           priority, bytes_received, buffer);
    status = EXIT_SUCCESS;

cleanup_close:
    if (mq_close(queue) == -1) {
        perror("mq_close");
        status = EXIT_FAILURE;
    }
    /*
     * ④ Remove the name from the kernel.  This marks the queue for
     * destruction once all openers close descriptors.  Removing it here
     * in the receiver means the next sender run creates a brand-new queue
     * (preventing attribute mismatches and stale-message buildup).
     */
    if (mq_unlink(QUEUE_NAME) == -1 && errno != ENOENT) {
        perror("mq_unlink");
        status = EXIT_FAILURE;
    }
    return status;
}

#define _POSIX_C_SOURCE 200809L

#include <errno.h>
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <mqueue.h>
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <sys/stat.h>

/*
 * PROGRAM:     POSIX Message Queue Sender (mq_open / mq_send)
 * MECHANISM:   POSIX message queue (mqd_t) — named, kernel-persistent,
 *              priority-ordered, message-boundary-preserving IPC.
 * DESCRIPTION: The SENDER / CREATOR half of a POSIX message-queue demo.
 *              POSIX message queues are different from pipes/sockets because
 *              each call to mq_send() writes a DISCRETE message with a 32-bit
 *              priority value, and each call to mq_receive() reads exactly
 *              ONE such message — message boundaries are preserved by the
 *              kernel and higher-priority messages are delivered before
 *              lower-priority ones even if they were queued later.  This
 *              program opens (or creates) the queue "/ipc_posix_mq_demo" with
 *              known maxmsg/msgsize attributes, clears any leftover messages
 *              from a crashed prior run, then enqueues one Chinese greeting
 *              message with priority 5.  An optional command-line argument
 *              overrides the default message.  Link with -lrt on glibc.
 * USAGE:       1. Run the sender first (creates the queue):
 *                  ./posix_mq_sender [optional_message]
 *              2. In another terminal run the receiver to dequeue and print:
 *                  ./posix_mq_receiver
 *              Receiver removes the queue name after reading.
 * STEPS:       ① Validate argc + message length vs MESSAGE_SIZE
 *              ② open_queue(): create or reuse queue, harden attrs, drain stale msgs
 *              ③ mq_send() the payload with MESSAGE_PRIORITY
 *              ④ mq_close() the descriptor; on failure-only: mq_unlink()
 */

#define QUEUE_NAME      "/ipc_posix_mq_demo"  /* POSIX MQ name (leading /)     */
#define MAX_MESSAGES    10                    /* queue capacity for demo       */
#define MESSAGE_SIZE    256                   /* largest single message (bytes)*/
#define MESSAGE_PRIORITY 5U                   /* priority; 0 = lowest, 31 = hi  */

/*
 * recreate_queue — destroy and rebuild the queue with known attributes.
 *
 * Called by open_queue() only when the queue already exists but its
 * (mq_maxmsg, mq_msgsize) don't match what this demo expects.  Performs
 * mq_unlink() followed by mq_open(O_CREAT|O_EXCL) to get a fresh queue.
 *
 * Parameters:
 *   queue   — output; receives the newly opened mqd_t on success.
 *   created — output; set to `true` so the caller's cleanup knows whether
 *             we were the ones who instantiated the kernel object.
 *
 * Return: 0 on success, -1 on failure (errno set by the failing syscall;
 *         diagnostic already printed via perror).
 */
static int recreate_queue(mqd_t *queue, bool *created)
{
    struct mq_attr attr = {
        .mq_flags = 0,
        .mq_maxmsg = MAX_MESSAGES,
        .mq_msgsize = MESSAGE_SIZE,
        .mq_curmsgs = 0
    };

    if (mq_unlink(QUEUE_NAME) == -1 && errno != ENOENT) {
        perror("mq_unlink");
        return -1;
    }

    *queue = mq_open(QUEUE_NAME, O_CREAT | O_EXCL | O_RDWR | O_NONBLOCK,
                     S_IRUSR | S_IWUSR, &attr);
    if (*queue == (mqd_t)-1) {
        perror("mq_open");
        return -1;
    }
    *created = true;
    return 0;
}

/*
 * open_queue — open or create the demo queue with a known configuration.
 *
 * Strategy:
 *   1. Try to create the queue exclusively (O_CREAT|O_EXCL).  On success
 *      we are the owner and return immediately with *created = true.
 *   2. If EEXIST (queue left over from a prior run), open the existing one
 *      read-write and check its mq_getattr() attributes:
 *        • If attrs match → drain any leftover messages from prior runs
 *          (loop mq_receive() in non-blocking mode until EAGAIN) so the
 *          receiver sees only our new message.
 *        • If attrs differ → the queue was created with different
 *          parameters; close it and call recreate_queue() to blow it
 *          away and start from scratch.
 *
 * Parameters:
 *   queue   — output mqd_t on success.
 *   created — output flag: true if we created a fresh kernel object.
 *
 * Return: 0 on success, -1 on failure (diagnostic printed).
 */
static int open_queue(mqd_t *queue, bool *created)
{
    struct mq_attr wanted = {
        .mq_flags = 0,
        .mq_maxmsg = MAX_MESSAGES,
        .mq_msgsize = MESSAGE_SIZE,
        .mq_curmsgs = 0
    };

    *queue = mq_open(QUEUE_NAME, O_CREAT | O_EXCL | O_RDWR | O_NONBLOCK,
                     S_IRUSR | S_IWUSR, &wanted);
    if (*queue != (mqd_t)-1) {
        *created = true;
        return 0;
    }
    if (errno != EEXIST) {
        perror("mq_open");
        return -1;
    }

    /* Queue already exists; reuse it if attributes match our protocol. */
    *queue = mq_open(QUEUE_NAME, O_RDWR | O_NONBLOCK);
    if (*queue == (mqd_t)-1) {
        perror("mq_open existing queue");
        return -1;
    }

    struct mq_attr actual;
    if (mq_getattr(*queue, &actual) == -1) {
        perror("mq_getattr");
        mq_close(*queue);
        return -1;
    }
    if (actual.mq_maxmsg != MAX_MESSAGES ||
        actual.mq_msgsize != MESSAGE_SIZE) {
        if (mq_close(*queue) == -1)
            perror("mq_close");
        return recreate_queue(queue, created);
    }

    /*
     * Drain stale messages left by a crashed receiver/sender from the
     * previous demo run.  Opened with O_NONBLOCK so the drain loop
     * terminates on EAGAIN (queue empty) rather than blocking forever.
     */
    char stale[MESSAGE_SIZE];
    for (;;) {
        if (mq_receive(*queue, stale, sizeof(stale), NULL) >= 0)
            continue;
        if (errno == EINTR)
            continue;
        if (errno != EAGAIN) {
            perror("mq_receive stale message");
            mq_close(*queue);
            return -1;
        }
        break;
    }
    return 0;
}

int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
    if (argc > 2) {
        fprintf(stderr, "用法: %s [消息]\n", argv[0]);
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    const char *message = argc == 2 ? argv[1] : "来自 POSIX 消息队列的问候";
    size_t length = strlen(message);
    if (length > MESSAGE_SIZE) {
        fprintf(stderr, "消息过长：最多 %d 字节\n", MESSAGE_SIZE);
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    mqd_t queue = (mqd_t)-1;
    bool created = false;
    if (open_queue(&queue, &created) == -1)
        return EXIT_FAILURE;

    int result = EXIT_SUCCESS;
    bool sent = false;
    /*
     * mq_send() enqueues a discrete message with explicit length and
     * priority.  Unlike SOCK_STREAM pipes/sockets, here the kernel
     * preserves the exact byte count per message so the reader can tell
     * where one message ends and the next begins without additional
     * framing.  Retry on EINTR; any other errno is fatal for this demo.
     */
    while (mq_send(queue, message, length, MESSAGE_PRIORITY) == -1) {
        if (errno == EINTR)
            continue;
        perror("mq_send");
        result = EXIT_FAILURE;
        break;
    }

    if (result == EXIT_SUCCESS) {
        sent = true;
        printf("已发送：%s（优先级 %u）\n", message, MESSAGE_PRIORITY);
    }

    if (mq_close(queue) == -1) {
        perror("mq_close");
        result = EXIT_FAILURE;
    }
    /*
     * Only remove the queue on the FAILURE path when we were the creator.
     * On success the queue must stay around for the receiver to open and
     * consume; if we unlink it prematurely the receiver gets ENOENT when
     * it tries to mq_open().
     */
    if (!sent && created &&
        mq_unlink(QUEUE_NAME) == -1 && errno != ENOENT) {
        perror("mq_unlink");
    }
    return result;
}

#define _XOPEN_SOURCE 700

#include <errno.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <sys/ipc.h>
#include <sys/msg.h>
#include <sys/stat.h>
#include <unistd.h>

/*
 * PROGRAM:     System V Message Queue Receiver (msgget / msgrcv / msgctl IPC_RMID)
 * MECHANISM:   System V message queue — identified by a SysV key_t derived via
 *              ftok(path, proj_id), with long `mtype` filtering on receive.
 * DESCRIPTION: The RECEIVER / CLEANER half of the System V MQ demo.
 *              Re-derives the same SysV key as the sender by ftok()-ing the
 *              same path (./sysv_mq_sender, the sibling executable) with the
 *              same PROJ_ID = 42, then msgget()s the EXISTING queue (no
 *              IPC_CREAT — if the sender hasn't created it yet, we bail with
 *              ENOENT because SysV MQs have no inherent "wait for the other
 *              end to appear" blocking semantics on open).  Once attached,
 *              we block in msgrcv(..., msgtyp = MESSAGE_TYPE, msgflg = 0)
 *              which will: (a) filter to only messages whose mtype matches
 *              MESSAGE_TYPE (== 1); (b) return the oldest such message in
 *              FIFO order; (c) sleep waiting for a matching message if none
 *              are present.  After printing the message the program calls
 *              msgctl(id, IPC_RMID, NULL) which DESTROYS the kernel object
 *              immediately — even if other processes still have it open
 *              (contrast with POSIX MQ / FIFO unlink which marks names only).
 * USAGE:       1. ./sysv_mq_sender [message]   in terminal A (creates + sends)
 *              2. ./sysv_mq_receiver           in terminal B (reads + destroys)
 *              Diagnostic: `ipcs -q` shows live SysV message queues; use
 *              `ipcrm -Q <hex_key>` or `ipcrm -q <id>` to clean leaks.
 * STEPS:       ① ftok("../sysv_mq_sender path", PROJ_ID) for key
 *              ② msgget(NO IPC_CREAT) — fail with ENOENT if sender hasn't run
 *              ③ blocking msgrcv(msgtyp = MESSAGE_TYPE) until message arrives
 *              ④ print type + bytes, then msgctl(IPC_RMID) to destroy the queue
 */

#define PROJ_ID       42                   /* must match sysv_mq_sender.c    */
#define MESSAGE_TYPE  1L                   /* mtype the sender tagged msg w/ */
#define TEXT_SIZE     255                  /* max payload bytes per msg      */

/*
 * struct message — MUST match the sender's layout byte-for-byte.
 *
 * mtype is a required long at offset 0.  The remaining members are opaque
 * application payload; we happen to use a char[] containing a NUL-terminated
 * C string.  The size passed to msgrcv() is sizeof(text), not sizeof(struct).
 */
struct message {
    long mtype;
    char text[TEXT_SIZE];
};

int main(void)
{
    /*
     * ① Derive the same key_t as the sender.
     *
     * The sender used ftok(argv[0] = <path to sysv_mq_sender binary>, PROJ_ID=42).
     * Here on the receiver side we don't have argv[0] pointing at the sender,
     * so we try the two most likely filesystem locations the demo user will
     * actually have:
     *   a) "./sysv_mq_sender" — both binaries live in the same directory.
     *   b) If that doesn't exist we use our own argv[0]-equivalent via
     *      "/proc/self/exe" on Linux would work, but for portability we
     *      simply retry the path "./sysv_mq_sender"; if the user renamed
     *      the sender binary they'll get a diagnostic explaining it.
     *
     * ftok() only needs the file to EXIST (st_dev + st_ino); it does not
     * need to be openable for reading or writing.
     */
    const char *sender_path = "./sysv_mq_sender";
    key_t key = ftok(sender_path, PROJ_ID);
    if (key == -1) {
        /*
         * Retry with the receiver's own binary as a last-ditch fallback so
         * the demo still works if the user accidentally swapped binaries.
         * This at least avoids giving the user a "no such file" when the
         * sender used its own binary (if both sender + receiver use the
         * SAME receiver binary ftok target, we still connect successfully
         * because ftok() results are identical for identical paths).
         */
        key = ftok("./sysv_mq_receiver", PROJ_ID);
        if (key == -1) {
            fprintf(stderr,
                    "ftok(\"%s\", %d) 失败：请确保先在同目录下编译好 sysv_mq_sender\n"
                    "    原始错误: %s\n",
                    sender_path, PROJ_ID, strerror(errno));
            return EXIT_FAILURE;
        }
    }

    /*
     * ② Attach to the existing queue.
     *
     * flags = S_IRUSR | S_IWUSR (no IPC_CREAT).  If the sender has not
     * created the queue, msgget() returns ENOENT — a clear diagnostic
     * is better than silently creating an empty queue (which would then
     * block forever in msgrcv with no incoming writer).
     */
    int id = msgget(key, S_IRUSR | S_IWUSR);
    if (id == -1) {
        if (errno == ENOENT)
            fprintf(stderr,
                    "未找到 System V 消息队列：请先运行 ./sysv_mq_sender 创建队列\n");
        else
            perror("msgget");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    struct message msg;
    ssize_t bytes = -1;
    int status = EXIT_FAILURE;

    /*
     * ③ msgrcv() — fetch one message matching our filter.
     *
     * msgrcv(msgid, msgp, msgsz, msgtyp, msgflg) filtering rules for msgtyp:
     *    msgtyp == 0         → return the oldest message on the queue (any type)
     *    msgtyp >  0         → return the oldest message with mtype == msgtyp
     *    msgtyp <  0 (abs)   → return the oldest message with mtype <= |msgtyp|
     *                          (the "low-numbered-priority-first" use case).
     * We ask for exactly MESSAGE_TYPE (== 1), matching what the sender sent.
     * msgflg = 0 → blocking, no MSG_NOERROR truncation.
     *
     * MSG_NOERROR behaviour (NOT used here): if we had passed MSG_NOERROR,
     * a payload larger than msgsz bytes would be silently truncated instead
     * of failing with E2BIG.  We avoid that because silent truncation hides
     * bugs during learning.
     */
    for (;;) {
        bytes = msgrcv(id, &msg, sizeof(msg.text), MESSAGE_TYPE, 0);
        if (bytes >= 0)
            break;
        if (errno == EINTR)
            continue;
        if (errno == E2BIG) {
            fprintf(stderr,
                    "收到的消息超过缓冲区 %zu 字节，请增大 TEXT_SIZE\n",
                    sizeof(msg.text));
        } else {
            perror("msgrcv");
        }
        /* After any receive error we still try IPC_RMID via cleanup. */
        goto cleanup_destroy;
    }

    /*
     * Sender memcpy()s a NUL-terminated C string, so bytes includes the
     * trailing '\0' — we can safely print with %s.  For robustness in case
     * the sender was modified to NOT include NUL, we also force-terminate
     * at index min(bytes, sizeof(text)-1).
     */
    if (bytes >= (ssize_t)sizeof(msg.text))
        bytes = (ssize_t)sizeof(msg.text) - 1;
    msg.text[bytes] = '\0';
    printf("收到消息（类型 %ld，%zd 字节）：%s\n",
           msg.mtype, bytes, msg.text);
    status = EXIT_SUCCESS;

cleanup_destroy:
    /*
     * ④ Destroy the queue.  msgctl(IPC_RMID) takes effect immediately on
     * the kernel object: any further msgsnd/msgrcv calls by other processes
     * will fail with EIDRM (identifier removed), and the memory is reclaimed
     * right away.  This is intentionally more aggressive than POSIX MQ's
     * mq_unlink() (which is a name-removal operation) because SysV IPC
     * objects have no reference-counted file descriptor keeping them alive;
     * without explicit IPC_RMID they leak until the next reboot (or an
     * ipcrm command).  IGNORING EINVAL here means we tolerate double-RMID
     * from signal handlers or races harmlessly.
     */
    if (msgctl(id, IPC_RMID, NULL) == -1 && errno != EINVAL && errno != EIDRM) {
        perror("msgctl IPC_RMID");
        status = EXIT_FAILURE;
    }
    return status;
}

#define _XOPEN_SOURCE 700

#include <errno.h>
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <sys/ipc.h>
#include <sys/msg.h>
#include <sys/stat.h>
#include <unistd.h>

/*
 * PROGRAM:     System V Message Queue Sender (msgget / msgsnd / msgctl)
 * MECHANISM:   System V message queue — kernel-persistent SysV IPC object
 *              identified by `key_t`, with long `mtype` message tags that
 *              let receivers filter by type rather than strict priority.
 * DESCRIPTION: The SENDER / CREATOR half of the System V message-queue demo.
 *              System V MQs differ from POSIX MQs in several subtle ways:
 *              (1) objects live in a SysV IPC namespace keyed by a (path, proj_id)
 *              tuple generated via ftok(), not the filesystem-like "/name" form;
 *              (2) each message is tagged with a POSITIVE long `mtype` that is
 *              used for type-based filtering on the receive side rather than
 *              a strict numeric priority; (3) capacity limits are controlled
 *              by the `MSGMNI`, `MSGMAX`, `MSGMNB` sysctls, not per-open attr;
 *              (4) cleanup is msgctl(IPC_RMID), not unlink().  The program
 *              derives the key from our own executable path + PROJ_ID = 42,
 *              msgget()s the queue (IPC_CREAT|IPC_EXCL first, falling back to
 *              reuse if it exists), clears any leftover messages from prior
 *              runs via a non-blocking drain loop, then msgsnd()s a single
 *              type=1 text message.  An optional argv[1] overrides the default.
 * USAGE:       1. Run the sender (creates the queue):
 *                  ./sysv_mq_sender [optional_message]
 *              2. In another terminal run the receiver (reads + IPC_RMID):
 *                  ./sysv_mq_receiver
 *              Use `ipcs -q` to inspect leaked SysV MQs after a crash, and
 *              `ipcrm -Q <key>` to clean them up by hand.
 * STEPS:       ① Validate argv + message length vs TEXT_SIZE
 *              ② ftok(argv[0], PROJ_ID) to obtain the SysV key
 *              ③ msgget() to create/reuse the queue; drain stale msgs
 *              ④ msgsnd() one type = MESSAGE_TYPE message
 *              ⑤ On failure-only: msgctl(IPC_RMID) if we created it
 */

#define PROJ_ID       42                   /* arbitrary non-zero proj_id      */
#define MESSAGE_TYPE  1L                   /* mtype for our demo message     */
#define TEXT_SIZE     255                  /* max data bytes per msgsnd      */

/*
 * struct message — on-the-wire layout for System V msgsnd()/msgrcv().
 *
 * The SysV MQ API REQUIRES the first member of every user-space message
 * struct to be a `long mtype` with a strictly positive (>0) value.  The
 * bytes that follow (here `text`) are the arbitrary-length application
 * payload, up to the system-wide MSGMAX limit (typical Linux default: 8192
 * bytes per message including mtype).  The msgsz argument to msgsnd/msgrcv
 * is the size of the payload ONLY (sizeof text), NOT sizeof the whole struct.
 */
struct message {
    long mtype;                            /* mandatory positive type tag    */
    char text[TEXT_SIZE];                  /* free-form payload bytes        */
};

int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
    if (argc > 2) {
        fprintf(stderr, "用法: %s [消息]\n", argv[0]);
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    const char *payload = argc == 2 ? argv[1] : "来自 System V 消息队列的问候";
    size_t length = strlen(payload);
    if (length >= TEXT_SIZE) {
        fprintf(stderr, "消息过长：最多 %d 字节\n", TEXT_SIZE - 1);
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    /*
     * ① ftok() — derive a SysV IPC key from (path, proj_id).
     *
     * ftok() has well-known quirks worth understanding:
     *   • It uses the pathname's st_dev (filesystem) + st_ino (inode) +
     *     the low 8 bits of proj_id as the key source.
     *   • If the path is deleted and recreated between sender and receiver,
     *     the inode may change and the two sides get DIFFERENT keys →
     *     they won't see the same queue.  Using argv[0] (our own binary)
     *     is reasonable for a demo because a freshly compiled binary has
     *     a stable inode for the duration of the demo session.
     *   • proj_id must be non-zero.  42 is a traditional demo value.
     */
    key_t key = ftok(argv[0], PROJ_ID);
    if (key == -1) {
        perror("ftok");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    /*
     * ② msgget() — create or attach to the SysV MQ.
     *
     * First try IPC_CREAT|IPC_EXCL to become the exclusive creator
     * (guarantees empty queue on first run).  If that fails with EEXIST
     * (leftover queue from a crash), we reopen with just IPC_CREAT to
     * attach to the existing object and drain any stale messages.
     * 0600 = S_IRUSR|S_IWUSR (owner read/write, no group/other access).
     */
    int id = msgget(key, IPC_CREAT | IPC_EXCL | S_IRUSR | S_IWUSR);
    bool created = false;
    if (id != -1) {
        created = true;
    } else if (errno == EEXIST) {
        id = msgget(key, IPC_CREAT | S_IRUSR | S_IWUSR);
        if (id == -1) {
            perror("msgget reuse");
            return EXIT_FAILURE;
        }

        /*
         * Drain stale messages left by a prior receiver crash.
         * IPC_NOWAIT makes msgrcv return -1 with errno = ENOMSG when the
         * queue is empty instead of blocking forever.  We loop until
         * empty.  The filter type 0 means "give the next message regardless
         * of its mtype".
         */
        struct message stale;
        for (;;) {
            if (msgrcv(id, &stale, sizeof(stale.text), 0, IPC_NOWAIT) >= 0)
                continue;
            if (errno == EINTR)
                continue;
            if (errno != ENOMSG) {
                perror("msgrcv drain stale");
                return EXIT_FAILURE;
            }
            break;
        }
    } else {
        perror("msgget create");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    struct message msg = { .mtype = MESSAGE_TYPE };
    memcpy(msg.text, payload, length + 1U);              /* include NUL terminator */

    int status = EXIT_SUCCESS;
    bool sent = false;
    /*
     * ③ msgsnd() — enqueue a single type-tagged message.
     *
     * 4th argument `msgflg` = 0 → block if the queue is currently full
     * (kernel enforces the queue's MSGMNB byte limit).  Retry EINTR; any
     * other failure is fatal for this demo.
     */
    while (msgsnd(id, &msg, length + 1U, 0) == -1) {
        if (errno == EINTR)
            continue;
        perror("msgsnd");
        status = EXIT_FAILURE;
        break;
    }
    if (status == EXIT_SUCCESS) {
        sent = true;
        printf("已发送（类型 %ld）：%s\n", MESSAGE_TYPE, payload);
    }

    /*
     * On the FAILURE path only: if we were the exclusive creator, remove
     * the kernel object so a fresh queue is instantiated next time.
     * On SUCCESS we MUST NOT remove it — the receiver hasn't read it yet.
     */
    if (!sent && created && msgctl(id, IPC_RMID, NULL) == -1) {
        perror("msgctl IPC_RMID");
    }
    return status;
}

#define _POSIX_C_SOURCE 200809L

#include <errno.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <unistd.h>

/*
 * PROGRAM:     Signal IPC Receiver (sigaction SA_SIGINFO + sigsuspend)
 * MECHANISM:   POSIX realtime signal with SA_SIGINFO 3-arg handler —
 *              sigval payload is read from siginfo_t::si_value, and delivery
 *              is synchronized via sigsuspend() to avoid the classic
 *              "check-then-wait" TOCTOU race.
 * DESCRIPTION: The RECEIVER half of the signal-based IPC demo.  Realtime
 *              signals are by default TERMinable dispositions, so we first
 *              install a handler via sigaction() with the SA_SIGINFO flag so
 *              the kernel delivers the payload through a `siginfo_t *`.  A
 *              critical subtlety: if a signal arrives BETWEEN the moment we
 *              check `signal_received == 0` and the moment we start sleeping
 *              (e.g. a plain pause() call), we'd miss the wakeup and hang
 *              forever.  POSIX solves this race by letting us BLOCK the
 *              signal during setup, then use `sigsuspend(new_mask)` to
 *              ATOMICALLY unblock + sleep until a signal arrives.  Only 2
 *              flags are "async-signal-safe" for setting inside the handler:
 *              `volatile sig_atomic_t` — which is why the two variables below
 *              carry both qualifiers.  After sigsuspend returns we print the
 *              int payload and exit.
 * USAGE:       1. ./signal_receiver            prints PID, blocks waiting
 *              2. ./signal_sender <PID> [int]  delivers SIGRTMIN+1
 *              The receiver exits after printing the first such signal.
 * STEPS:       ① Reserve SIGRTMIN+1 (validate range)
 *              ② sigprocmask(SIG_BLOCK, {SIGRTMIN+1}) — block signal during setup
 *              ③ sigaction(SA_SIGINFO) — install the 3-arg handler
 *              ④ Print PID; fflush so user sees it before we sleep
 *              ⑤ Loop: while (!signal_received) sigsuspend(mask_without_sig)
 *              ⑥ Restore original signal mask, then print the payload.
 */

/*
 * Shared flag + payload between the signal handler and main().
 *
 * `volatile` tells the compiler "this variable changes outside normal
 * control flow" — without it, main()'s optimizer could hoist the initial
 * read of `signal_received` out of the while loop and spin forever on a
 * stale register copy.  `sig_atomic_t` is the only ISO C type the standard
 * guarantees can be read/written atomically with respect to an asynchronous
 * signal handler on the same thread.
 */
static volatile sig_atomic_t signal_received = 0;
static volatile sig_atomic_t received_value = 0;

/*
 * handle_signal — 3-argument SA_SIGINFO signal handler.
 *
 * Invoked by the kernel asynchronously when SIGRTMIN+1 is delivered to
 * this process.  Inside a signal handler ONLY a very short list of POSIX
 * functions ("async-signal-safe functions" — see signal-safety(7)) may be
 * called; printf() / malloc() / anything that takes a lock is FORBIDDEN.
 * So the handler does the MINIMUM possible work: copy si_value.sival_int
 * into a sig_atomic_t variable and flip the flag that main polls.  All
 * three parameters are only here to satisfy the SA_SIGINFO prototype;
 * signum & context are explicitly unused.
 */
static void handle_signal(int signum, siginfo_t *info, void *context)
{
    (void)signum;
    (void)context;

    /* Async-signal-safe assignments only inside this block. */
    if (info != NULL)
        received_value = info->si_value.sival_int;
    signal_received = 1;
}

int main(void)
{
    const int target_signal = SIGRTMIN + 1;
    if (target_signal > SIGRTMAX) {
        fprintf(stderr, "当前系统没有可用的目标实时信号\n");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    /*
     * ① BLOCK the target signal BEFORE we install the handler.
     *
     * Blocking a signal means the kernel appends it to our per-thread
     * pending-signal set instead of invoking the handler.  Why block it
     * here?  It closes the window where the signal arrives AFTER we've
     * installed the handler but BEFORE we've entered the sigsuspend()
     * loop — if we didn't block, such a signal would be delivered
     * immediately, set signal_received=1, but we'd never have lost any
     * data anyway; the REAL win is that sigsuspend() REQUIRES that the
     * caller has the signal currently blocked to give atomic
     * "unblock + sleep" semantics.  old_mask receives the previous mask
     * so we can restore it at the end.
     */
    sigset_t blocked;
    sigset_t old_mask;
    if (sigemptyset(&blocked) == -1 ||
        sigaddset(&blocked, target_signal) == -1 ||
        sigprocmask(SIG_BLOCK, &blocked, &old_mask) == -1) {
        perror("准备信号掩码");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    /*
     * ② Install the SA_SIGINFO 3-argument handler.
     *
     * Without SA_SIGINFO the kernel invokes a 1-arg (int signum) handler
     * that has NO access to si_value / si_code / si_pid / si_uid.  With
     * the flag we get a siginfo_t* describing exactly who sent the signal
     * and what payload they attached.  action.sa_mask is left empty (we
     * don't want to block any other signals inside the handler).
     */
    struct sigaction action = {0};
    action.sa_sigaction = handle_signal;
    action.sa_flags = SA_SIGINFO;
    if (sigemptyset(&action.sa_mask) == -1 ||
        sigaction(target_signal, &action, NULL) == -1) {
        perror("sigaction");
        sigprocmask(SIG_SETMASK, &old_mask, NULL);
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    /*
     * Print our PID for the user to pass to ./signal_sender.
     * stdout is usually line-buffered when attached to a tty, so the '\n'
     * would flush it; nonetheless we call fflush() explicitly so the
     * output appears even if stdout got redirected to a file (fully
     * buffered).  This is important: otherwise the user might think the
     * program is hanging before it even waits.
     */
    printf("接收端 PID：%ld，等待信号 SIGRTMIN+1\n", (long)getpid());
    if (fflush(stdout) == EOF) {
        perror("fflush");
        sigprocmask(SIG_SETMASK, &old_mask, NULL);
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    /*
     * ③ sigsuspend() — the atomic "unblock & sleep" primitive.
     *
     * wait_mask starts as the pre-setup mask (usually empty), then we
     * REMOVE the target signal from it.  When sigsuspend(&wait_mask) is
     * invoked:
     *   Step A: atomically swap our signal mask to `wait_mask` → which
     *           enables (unblocks) target_signal.
     *   Step B: immediately put the thread to sleep until any unblocked
     *           signal is delivered to a handler or terminates the process.
     *
     * The "atomic" guarantee means a signal arriving between A and B
     * can't be lost — which the obvious-but-wrong alternative of:
     *        sigprocmask(unblock) → THEN pause()
     * would lose if the signal fires between the two syscalls.
     *
     * sigsuspend() always returns -1 with errno set; EINTR means a
     * handler successfully ran and returned, so we check signal_received.
     */
    sigset_t wait_mask = old_mask;
    if (sigdelset(&wait_mask, target_signal) == -1) {
        perror("sigdelset");
        sigprocmask(SIG_SETMASK, &old_mask, NULL);
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }
    while (!signal_received) {
        if (sigsuspend(&wait_mask) == -1 && errno != EINTR) {
            perror("sigsuspend");
            sigprocmask(SIG_SETMASK, &old_mask, NULL);
            return EXIT_FAILURE;
        }
    }

    /*
     * ④ Restore original signal mask (re-blocks target_signal if the
     * pre-setup environment had it blocked) and print the payload that
     * the handler captured into received_value.
     */
    if (sigprocmask(SIG_SETMASK, &old_mask, NULL) == -1) {
        perror("sigprocmask restore");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }
    printf("收到信号，携带整数：%d\n", (int)received_value);
    return EXIT_SUCCESS;
}

#define _POSIX_C_SOURCE 200809L

#include <ctype.h>
#include <errno.h>
#include <limits.h>
#include <signal.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <unistd.h>

/*
 * PROGRAM:     Signal IPC Sender (sigqueue / SIGRTMIN+1 with int payload)
 * MECHANISM:   POSIX real-time signal + `sigqueue()` — kernel-queued,
 *              in-order signal delivery with a small `union sigval` payload.
 * DESCRIPTION: The SIGNAL-SENDING half of a two-process signal-based IPC
 *              demo.  Standard (non-realtime) POSIX signals like SIGUSR1 are
 *              lossy: sending the same signal N times while it's blocked
 *              results in only ONE delivery (pending set is a bitmask, not
 *              a queue).  Real-time signals (SIGRTMIN..SIGRTMAX) fix that by
 *              actually queueing every `sigqueue()` up to the per-process
 *              RLIMIT_SIGPENDING cap.  Additionally `sigqueue()` lets us
 *              attach a tiny `union sigval` payload (either a pointer or an
 *              int) that the receiver's handler can read from
 *              `siginfo_t->si_value`.  Here we send SIGRTMIN+1 with either
 *              the user-provided integer from argv[2] or 0 as a default.
 * USAGE:       1. In terminal A start the receiver, it prints its PID:
 *                  ./signal_receiver
 *              2. In terminal B send it a signal with an int payload:
 *                  ./signal_sender <RECEIVER_PID> [integer_payload]
 *              e.g.  ./signal_sender 12345 42
 * STEPS:       ① Strict-parse argv[1] as PID (1..INT_MAX) and argv[2] as int
 *              ② Pick a realtime signal: SIGRTMIN + 1 (don't use +0, glibc
 *                 pthreads reserves SIGRTMIN itself internally)
 *              ③ Build a union sigval with the sival_int payload
 *              ④ sigqueue() the signal, retry EINTR
 *              ⑤ Report which PID / payload we sent
 */

/*
 * parse_long_strict — parse a base-10 integer rejecting whitespace / trailing
 * garbage / range errors.
 *
 * strtol() alone silently accepts leading whitespace and/or trailing garbage
 * characters, both of which would let the user pass e.g. "123abc" or "  42"
 * as a "number".  This wrapper tightens input validation so only pure
 * "fully numeric" strings are accepted.
 *
 * Parameters:
 *   text     — NUL-terminated string to parse.
 *   minimum  — lowest acceptable parsed value (inclusive).
 *   maximum  — highest acceptable parsed value (inclusive).
 *   value    — output location; only written on success.
 *
 * Return: 0 on success, -1 on any parse / range error (errno set by strtol
 * where applicable).
 */
static int parse_long_strict(const char *text, long minimum, long maximum,
                             long *value)
{
    if (text[0] == '\0' || isspace((unsigned char)text[0]))
        return -1;

    errno = 0;
    char *end = NULL;
    long parsed = strtol(text, &end, 10);
    if (errno == ERANGE || *end != '\0' ||
        parsed < minimum || parsed > maximum) {
        return -1;
    }
    *value = parsed;
    return 0;
}

int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
    if (argc < 2 || argc > 3) {
        fprintf(stderr, "用法: %s PID [整数]\n", argv[0]);
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    /*
     * ① Parse and validate the target PID.
     *
     * The kernel defines pid_t as a signed int on Linux; PIDs start at 1
     * (0 is reserved for the scheduler's idle task, PID 1 is init).  We
     * reject anything outside [1, INT_MAX], and also sanity-check the
     * (long)→(pid_t) round-trip because posix allows pid_t to be narrower
     * than long on exotic platforms.
     */
    long parsed_pid;
    if (parse_long_strict(argv[1], 1, INT_MAX, &parsed_pid) == -1) {
        fprintf(stderr, "无效 PID：%s\n", argv[1]);
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }
    pid_t pid = (pid_t)parsed_pid;
    if ((long)pid != parsed_pid) {
        fprintf(stderr, "PID 超出当前系统范围\n");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    /* ② Parse optional int payload; absent means 0. */
    long parsed_value = 0;
    if (argc == 3 &&
        parse_long_strict(argv[2], INT_MIN, INT_MAX, &parsed_value) == -1) {
        fprintf(stderr, "无效整数：%s\n", argv[2]);
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    /*
     * ③ Choose a realtime signal number.
     *
     * NOTE: We deliberately use SIGRTMIN + 1, not SIGRTMIN itself.  On
     * glibc + NPTL (the native Linux threads library), SIGRTMIN and
     * SIGRTMIN+1 are RESERVED internally by pthread_cancel() and other
     * threading support code.  The portable API-guaranteed available
     * range starts at SIGRTMIN+2 for glibc in practice; we still allow
     * SIGRTMIN+1 here only because neither binary spawns any threads,
     * and then verify the result <= SIGRTMAX so we never go out of
     * range on platforms with fewer realtime signals.
     */
    const int target_signal = SIGRTMIN + 1;
    if (target_signal > SIGRTMAX) {
        fprintf(stderr, "当前系统没有可用的目标实时信号\n");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    /*
     * ④ Build the `union sigval` payload and sigqueue() it.
     *
     * union sigval has two members:
     *     int         sival_int    — plain integer for small values
     *     void       *sival_ptr    — pointer; only meaningful within the
     *                                SAME address space (useless for IPC)
     * So for cross-process delivery we always use sival_int.  Contrast with
     * kill() — which is (pid, signo, 0) with NO payload at all — sigqueue()
     * is a strict superset specifically for carrying an extra 4/8 bytes.
     *
     * Retry on EINTR (sigqueue can be interrupted by other signals); any
     * other errno is fatal for the demo.  Common failures to expect:
     *     ESRCH   — no such PID (receiver hasn't started / already exited)
     *     EAGAIN  — per-process RLIMIT_SIGPENDING queue capacity exhausted
     *     EPERM   — credentials don't allow signalling the target UID
     */
    union sigval value;
    value.sival_int = (int)parsed_value;
    while (sigqueue(pid, target_signal, value) == -1) {
        if (errno == EINTR)
            continue;
        perror("sigqueue");
        return EXIT_FAILURE;
    }

    printf("已向 PID %ld 发送 SIGRTMIN+1，整数为 %d\n",
           (long)pid, value.sival_int);
    return EXIT_SUCCESS;
}

children.topic: Linux 进程间通信（IPC）学习验证 — 开发日志

children.detail:
• 1. 匿名管道 & 命名管道 FIFO
